templates.pattern: A straight conductor of length [L] m carries a current of [I] A in a magnetic field of flux density [B] T. Calculate the magnetic flux density needed to produce a force of [F] N on the conductor in T.
templates.explanation:
From F = BIL:
B = F ÷ (I × L)
= [F] ÷ ([I] × [L])
= [F] ÷ [I*L]
= [RESULT] T

Magnetic flux density is measured in tesla (T). It tells us the strength of the magnetic field at a point.

templates.pattern: A charged particle of charge [Q] C moves at [V] m/s perpendicular to a magnetic field of flux density [B] T. Calculate the magnetic force on the particle in newtons.
templates.explanation:
Force on moving charge = BQv
= [B] × [Q] × [V]
= [RESULT] N

This force is always perpendicular to both the velocity and the magnetic field. It causes charged particles to move in circular paths in uniform magnetic fields.

templates.pattern: A conductor of length [L] m moves at [V] m/s perpendicular to a magnetic field of flux density [B] T. Calculate the EMF induced in the conductor in volts.
templates.explanation:
Induced EMF = BLv
= [B] × [L] × [V]
= [RESULT] V

This is Faraday's Law in action. The faster the conductor moves and the stronger the field the greater the induced EMF. This is how generators produce electricity.

templates.pattern: A coil of [N] turns has a magnetic flux change of [DPHI] Wb in [T] seconds. Calculate the magnitude of the induced EMF in volts.
templates.explanation:
Induced EMF = N × ΔΦ ÷ t
= [N] × [DPHI] ÷ [T]
= [RESULT] V

This is Faraday's Law of electromagnetic induction. A greater number of turns, a faster flux change or a larger flux change all produce a greater induced EMF.

templates.pattern: A capacitor stores a charge of [Q] C when connected to a potential difference of [V] V. Calculate the capacitance of the capacitor in farads.
templates.explanation:
Capacitance = Charge ÷ Potential Difference
= C = Q ÷ V
= [Q] ÷ [V]
= [RESULT] F

Capacitance measures the ability of a component to store charge. The farad is a very large unit — most practical capacitors are measured in microfarads (μF) or picofarads (pF).

templates.pattern: A capacitor of capacitance [C] F is charged to a potential difference of [V] V. Calculate the energy stored in the capacitor in joules.
templates.explanation:
Energy stored = ½CV²
= 0.5 × [C] × [V]²
= 0.5 × [C] × [V*V]
= [RESULT] J

The energy stored increases with the square of voltage. Doubling the voltage quadruples the stored energy. Capacitors release this energy very rapidly — much faster than batteries.

templates.pattern: A capacitor of capacitance [C] F is connected in series with a resistor of resistance [R] Ω. Calculate the time constant of the RC circuit in seconds.
templates.explanation:
Time constant τ = R × C
= [R] × [C]
= [RESULT] s

The time constant is the time taken for the charge to fall to 37% of its initial value during discharge, or rise to 63% during charging. After 5 time constants the capacitor is considered fully charged or discharged.

templates.pattern: An AC supply has a peak voltage of [VP] V. Calculate the RMS voltage in volts.
templates.explanation:
RMS voltage = peak voltage ÷ √2
= [VP] ÷ √2
= [VP] ÷ 1.414
= [RESULT] V

The RMS voltage is the equivalent DC voltage that would deliver the same power. The UK mains supply has a peak voltage of about 325 V giving an RMS of 230 V.

templates.pattern: An AC supply has a peak current of [IP] A. Calculate the RMS current in amperes.
templates.explanation:
RMS current = peak current ÷ √2
= [IP] ÷ √2
= [IP] ÷ 1.414
= [RESULT] A

RMS current produces the same heating effect as an equivalent DC current. Power calculations using P = I²R should use RMS values not peak values.

templates.pattern: An AC power supply has a time period of [T] ms. Calculate the frequency of the supply in Hz.
templates.explanation:
Frequency = 1 ÷ period
= 1 ÷ ([T] ÷ 1000)
= 1000 ÷ [T]
= [RESULT] Hz

The UK mains frequency is 50 Hz giving a period of 20 ms. The USA uses 60 Hz. Frequency and period are always reciprocals of each other.
